items_missed: CLASSIFICATION NOTE (methodology call): the origin home is exactly 1800 sqft and the call did end in a virtual-tour/photo-upload route, but this is graded as a full_sales_call, not a walkthrough_scheduler. Erik delivered the complete pricing structure, the clock, and a dollarized estimate on the phone ('between the six and seven hour range with three guys on one truck... an estimated total of $2,142'), and only offered the walkthrough after the customer asked for it. Auto-crediting pricing/clock/estimate/Save Your Ass here would have hidden real behavior on three sections he worked and one he skipped entirely.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' confirmation. The closest thing was 'to get you a solid estimate sir to start I would just need to build up a profile for you' — that names the next step but sets no roadmap and no timeframe, so the customer never knew a 16-minute call was coming.
Never asked 'how are you today?' — went from 'Einstein Moving Company, this is Eric' straight to 'did you have a specific date in mind?'

SAVE YOUR ASS ENTIRELY ABSENT — 0/10, and the customer teed it up himself: 'there's a bunch of crap in there but I'm trying to get rid of most of that before we move out.' Erik answered 'Okay. Okay.' No prep-equals-shorter-move-equals-lower-bill framing, no consolidation examples, no take-a-carload tip. On a 4-bedroom, 80-85-box, two-story move with a loaded garage, this is the single most expensive omission on the call.

No Worries Damage Coverage never named and the $2,000 figure never stated. Erik referred only to 'the insurance that we placed on your move' — generic, unquantified, and delivered on a call where the customer's stated anxiety was 'I just don't want to be surprised.'

Packing services never raised at any point — not as a probe question, not as pricing. Erik established 80-85 boxes for a four-bedroom house and never asked who was packing them or quoted the packing rate plus materials. That is a probe miss and a revenue miss on the same beat.

No 'no deposit required' — never said, on a call where the customer volunteered he is comparison shopping ('I got to talk to my wife and she has somebody else given her an estimate'). No-deposit is the differentiator built for exactly that moment and it went unused.

No booking attempt. Erik put a target date in the system ('I've got you targeting the fourteenth') but never asked for the business — no 'we have availability, want to lock that in?' and no offer to hold the 14th while the customer talks to his wife. The call ended on 'we can kind of revisit the conversation from there.'

Estimate quoted below Erik's own stated typical band. He said 1800 sqft homes are 'usually between the six and a half to eight and a half hour range' and then set the quote at 'between the six and seven hour range' — under the floor of his own range, on a house with four bedrooms, three stand-up freezers, a washer/dryer, a large fridge, a two-piece China cabinet, a wall-mounted 70-inch TV plus three more TVs, and a garage full of boxes and a rolling toolbox. His justification ('I would still consider you to be kind of on the lower end of the spectrum') is not supported by the inventory he just collected. This is the exact manager-adjustment-downward pattern behind the 45-46% estimate accuracy number.

Stairs collected but never priced into the estimate. Both homes are two-story and Erik never explained that stairs add time — a variable that matters more than usual here because it works in both directions (origin upstairs load, destination upstairs unload).

Never asked about long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns, parking, or HOA/truck access at either address. On a 70-inch wall-mounted TV and a two-piece China cabinet, tight-turn risk should have been asked, not assumed.
Never asked about storage stops or additional stops.
Destination zip never captured — origin was confirmed to 75023, the McKinney drop-off never was.

Clock start never explained. The 2.5-hour minimum and 15-minute prorating were both delivered cleanly, but 'the clock starts on-site when we open the contract' was skipped, which is the piece that prevents a move-day dispute about drive time.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask — the reply request that was made ('just letting me know that you've uploaded everything') is about the upload link, not about verifying the move details.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' at the close, and business hours were never given — the customer had to prompt with 'what's the next step we gotta do?' to get the wrap-up.
top_strength: The discovery and the empathy pivot are genuinely strong, and they are why this call scored 48 instead of the low 30s. Erik ran a real room-by-room inventory rather than accepting a square-footage number and moving on — 'if you wouldn't mind Michael just kind of taking me throughout the house room by room and talking to me about the furniture items that we'll be moving for you' — and he stayed with it through a long, rambling, hard-to-follow answer without cutting the customer off. He then calibrated the box count instead of guessing at it: 'for a home in kind of the 1800 square foot range. We would usually see somewhere between maybe like seventy and ninety boxes. Does that feel like an accurate guess or way too little way too many?' — the single best technique on the call, because it anchors the customer and gets a confirmed number in one move. He also chased the specialty risk on his own initiative ('that's got glass on the front, I'm assuming' and 'is it two pieces as well the China cabinet?'). Best of all, he actually asked the stressor question — 'are there any specific stresser concerns anything like that you have about the moving process' — and when Michael said 'I have moved in twenty years... I don't know what to expect, I just don't want to be surprised,' Erik met it properly: 'when we start talking about apartment moves, people are moving every year but this will be a big life event for you guys. So I'll keep it as straightforward as I can for you.' That answer earned an unprompted compliment later in the call ('you do sound really different'), which is the clearest possible signal the rapport landed. The what's-included pitch was also complete and well-sequenced — truck, crew, fuel, taxes, insurance, blankets/pads/shrink wrap/bands, tools, appliance disconnect and reconnect, free service zone at both addresses, closing on 'you will see no additional or hidden fees of any type.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Erik got the perfect Save Your Ass opening handed to him and let it die. When Michael said 'there's a bunch of crap in there but I'm trying to get rid of most of that before we move out,' the answer needed to be: 'Michael, that is the best thing you can do for your own bill — everything you clear out or consolidate before we get there comes straight off the clock. Get the loose stuff out of drawers into boxes, get the kids' toys and the garden tools consolidated, take the photos off the walls, and anything small enough to fit in your car, take a carload over yourself. On a job this size that can easily save you an hour, which is $306 back in your pocket. Does that make sense?' That one paragraph is worth 10 rubric points, it directly serves the estimate-accuracy rock, and it costs 30 seconds. Second priority, and this is the one with money attached today: this call ended unbooked against a named competitor. Michael said his wife already has another estimate, and Erik never used the two tools built for that exact moment — no deposit and No Worries. He should have closed with 'There's no deposit and nothing to pay to hold a date, so I can put the 14th on the calendar right now and you lose nothing if you and your wife decide differently. And on the not-wanting-surprises piece — every move is covered by our No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage. That's included, not an add-on.' Also add Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee to the differentiator block — all three were absent, so the customer is comparing Einstein to the other quote on price alone, which is the one comparison we do not want. Third, estimate discipline: Erik stated the typical band as 6.5-8.5 hours and then quoted 6-7 — below his own floor — on a four-bedroom, two-story, 80-85-box move with three stand-up freezers and a full garage. If he genuinely believes this job is on the light end, the quote should sit at the bottom of the band (6.5-8), not underneath it. Underquoting to make the number look good on the phone is precisely how a move lands outside the 20% accuracy window and turns into a move-day surprise for the customer who just told us surprises are his one fear. Two things to fix in EMMA before the walkthrough: packing services were never discussed at all despite 80-85 boxes, and access/tight-turn conditions were never asked at either address — the 70-inch wall-mount and the two-piece China cabinet make that a real load-planning gap. Finally, Erik should proactively send the upload link with a deadline attached ('I'll text it over in the next five minutes — if you can get it back to me by Tuesday I can have your final number before you and your wife decide') so the walkthrough becomes a reason to come back rather than an open loop.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and unhurried — 'we're making some good progress here,' 'no worries at all man,' 'It's been a pleasure hanging out on the phone' — and he named the customer's twenty-year gap as 'a big life event for you guys' rather than plowing past it, which drew the unprompted compliment 'you do sound really different.'
